nameStory: This tiny alpine treasure gets its name from being a true mountain dweller - it's one of the smallest cinquefoils and lives exclusively above treeline in New Hampshire's White Mountains. The 'cinquefoil' part comes from French meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the typical five-leaflet pattern found in most species in this group. It was named after Edward Hutchins Robbins, a 19th-century botanist who studied New England's alpine plants.
description: Dwarf mountain cinquefoil is one of New England's rarest and most specialized plants - a tiny yellow-flowered perennial that grows only in the harsh alpine zone above treeline. This diminutive plant is nearly stemless and incredibly small, measuring just 2-4 centimeters across (about the size of a large coin). It hugs the ground tightly as a survival strategy against fierce mountain winds and extreme weather. You'll only find this botanical treasure in New Hampshire's White Mountains, making it one of the region's most exclusive alpine residents.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Incredibly small and nearly stemless, forming tight cushions only 2-4 cm across that hug the rocky ground like living coins scattered on the mountaintop

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five rounded petals that seem oversized for the tiny plant, blooming close to the ground on very short stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small compound leaves divided into three leaflets with silky hairs that feel soft to the touch and help protect against alpine conditions

idTips.label: Habitat Specialization
idTips.description: Found exclusively above treeline in rocky, exposed alpine areas where few other plants can survive the harsh mountain conditions

habitat: This ultra-specialized plant lives only in the alpine zone above treeline in New Hampshire's White Mountains, typically at elevations above 4,000 feet. Look for it in rocky, exposed areas with thin soils where it grows among cushion plants and other hardy alpine survivors. It thrives in the harsh conditions of mountain summits and ridges where fierce winds, extreme temperature swings, and intense UV radiation would kill most lowland plants.

seasonality.spring: Emerges slowly from snowmelt, with new growth appearing as tiny rosettes of silvery-green leaves pressed tight against the rocks.
seasonality.summer: Blooms during the brief alpine growing season, producing bright yellow flowers that stand out dramatically against the rocky landscape.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may take on slightly reddish tints as the plant prepares for the long alpine winter.
seasonality.winter: Completely buried under snow for many months, surviving in a dormant state beneath the protective snow cover.

funFact: This tiny plant is so rare that there are only about 20 recorded observations in all of New England - making it exponentially rarer than finding a four-leaf clover, and you can only search for it by hiking to some of the most challenging terrain in the region!
confusionNotes: Its extremely limited habitat above treeline makes confusion unlikely - if you're not on an alpine summit in the White Mountains, you're not looking at this plant. Other small alpine plants in the area lack the distinctive yellow five-petaled flowers and cushion growth form.
contextualKnowledge: This plant represents New England's connection to Arctic flora - many of our alpine plants are remnants from the last ice age that retreated to mountain peaks as the climate warmed. It's considered globally rare and is of significant conservation concern due to climate change and foot traffic impacts.
compareHints: Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone. Common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil grow much larger and spread along trails and fields at lower elevations. The extreme size difference and exclusive high-altitude habitat make this species unmistakable among New England's cinquefoils.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
